title: Homodyne Unravelling and Parameter Estimation in Squeezed Thermal Baths
authors: Eoin O'Connor, Francesco Albarelli, Marco G. Genoni
abstract: We derive an alternative formulation of the stochastic master equation describing the evolution of quantum systems continuously measured via homodyne detection in a squeezed-thermal environment. This formulation allows us to identify two distinct collapse operators, corresponding respectively to the monitored and unmonitored channels, and to express the quantum state evolution directly in terms of Kraus-like operators. As a consequence, it facilitates the application of advanced numerical methods that account for higher-order corrections and discrete-time monitoring, and it also enables the efficient numerical evaluation of Cramér-Rao bounds in parameter estimation problems. To demonstrate the latter, we evaluate the Fisher information of the continuous homodyne monitoring for qubit frequency estimation in the presence of a squeezed-thermal bath. Our results show that exponential scaling of the steady-state Fisher information rate with squeezing is retained even at non-zero temperature.
summary: This paper develops a novel stochastic master equation formulation for quantum systems measured in squeezed-thermal baths. By separating the evolution into monitored and unmonitored channels, it enables rigorous calculation of the Fisher information. The key finding is that environmental squeezing enhances the estimation precision, a scaling that persists even when thermal noise is present.
main_problem: The paper derives an alternative, mathematically clean formulation of the stochastic master equation (SME) for quantum systems undergoing continuous homodyne measurement in a squeezed-thermal environment.
main_result: The derived SME explicitly separates the evolution into unmonitored and monitored parts, and the analysis confirms that the Fisher information rate for parameter estimation retains exponential scaling with squeezing even at non-zero temperatures.
method: The authors use algebraic manipulation of the Lindblad superoperator to derive the alternative SME form, which allows the application of advanced numerical techniques and the evaluation of Cramér-Rao bounds.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum entity (e.g., a qubit) coupled to a Markovian squeezed-thermal bath, and the measurement process is continuous homodyne detection.
key_observables: Fisher information rate ($F_{hom}$), steady-state Fisher information rate, and the quantum state evolution ($ho_c$).
important_parameters: Squeezing parameter ($r$), thermal excitation number ($ ar{n}_{	ext{th}}$), and the measurement time $T$.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on specific identities involving the Lindblad superoperator and assumes the equivalence of conditional dynamics between the squeezed-thermal and vacuum-input models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of the homodyne Fisher information rate ($F_{hom}/T$) under varying thermal noise ($ ar{n}_{	ext{th}}$) and squeezing ($r$), comparing results against the Heisenberg Limit.
paper_structure: The paper first derives the alternative SME formulation, then applies this framework to the specific problem of qubit frequency estimation, culminating in the calculation and analysis of the Fisher information rate.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical tools for quantifying measurement-induced quantum enhancement in noisy environments, which is central to quantum sensing and quantum information processing.

The time-averaged homodyne Fisher information rate, Fhom/T of the frequency of a qubit coupled to a thermal environment for (a): different values of the thermal occupation at zero squeezing (r = 0); and (b): fixed thermal occupation (¯nth = 0.2) with different values of the squeezing parameter r. The black dashed line indicates the Heisenberg limit (HL), Fhom/T = 4T, which bounds the achievable Fisher information rate for Hamiltonian frequency estimation. The results were obtained by averaging over Ntraj = 105 trajectories in (a) and Ntraj = 2 × 104 trajectories in (b). In all simulations, ω/κ = 0.5 and the qubit is prepared in the ground state of σz.
